title: How a blockchain catches tampering
summary: See why changing one old record on a blockchain gets caught, even with nobody in charge.
objective: Predict what happens when someone edits an old blockchain record, and explain why the edit fails.

hook.prompt: A record of payments is copied on thousands of computers. Someone quietly changes one old payment on their own copy. What happens?

options.text: The change spreads to every other copy
options.feedback: The other copies don't follow one computer's edits. You'll see why in a moment.

options.text: The other computers spot it and ignore that copy
Nobody can tell, since it's just one old entry
options.feedback: It's easier to tell than you'd think: the record itself gives the edit away.

hook.explanation: No person has to notice. The record itself gives the edit away, thanks to a kind of fingerprint every block carries.

bricks.title: Every block has a fingerprint
bricks.body: A blockchain is a shared record book. Its records are grouped into **blocks**, and each block gets a **hash**: a short code calculated from everything inside it, like a fingerprint. The same contents always give the same hash. Change even one character and the hash comes out completely different.

term.definition: A short code calculated from a block's contents. Any change to the contents gives a completely different code.

visual.html:
Ana pays Ben 5 coinshasha3f9…
Ana pays Ben 50 coinshashe71c…

One extra character, a completely different hash (shortened here).
visual.alt: Two records that differ by one character, Ana pays Ben 5 coins and Ana pays Ben 50 coins, with completely different hashes: a3f9 and e71c.

bricks.prompt: A block says "Ana pays Ben 5 coins". Someone changes the 5 to 50. What happens to that block's hash?

options.text: It becomes a completely different code
Only one character of it changes, matching the edit
options.feedback: A hash isn't a copy of the contents. Any change, however small, gives a completely different code.

options.text: It stays the same, since only a number changed
options.feedback: The hash is calculated from everything in the block, numbers included, so any edit changes it.

bricks.hint: Recall what happens to a hash when even one character changes.
bricks.explanation: The hash is calculated from all of the block's contents. Changing 5 to 50 changes the contents, so the fingerprint comes out completely different.

bricks.prompt: Two computers each calculate the hash of the exact same block, character for character. What do they get?

options.text: The same hash
Two different hashes, one per computer
options.feedback: A hash isn't random or tied to a computer. The same contents always give the same hash.

options.text: It depends on which computer is faster
options.feedback: Speed doesn't matter. The hash depends only on the block's contents, so identical contents give identical hashes.

bricks.hint: What does the hash depend on?
bricks.explanation: Same contents in, same hash out. That's why any computer can recalculate a block's hash and check it.

bricks.title: Hashes link the blocks into a chain
bricks.body: Each block also stores the **hash of the block before it**. Those stored hashes link the blocks in order: Block 3 holds Block 2's hash, Block 2 holds Block 1's. The stored hash is part of the block, so it counts toward that block's own hash too. Edit an old block and its hash changes, so the next block's stored link no longer matches.

visual.html:
Block 1Previous: noneHash a3f9
Block 2Previous: a3f9Hash 7c1e
Block 3Previous: 7c1eHash 2b8d
visual.alt: Three blocks in a row. Block 1 has hash a3f9. Block 2 stores previous a3f9 and has hash 7c1e. Block 3 stores previous 7c1e and has hash 2b8d.

bricks.prompt: Someone edited a payment in Block 2, so its hash is now 9f04. Tap the block whose stored link no longer matches.

visual.html:
Block 1Previous: noneHash a3f9
Block 2EditedPrevious: a3f9Hash 9f04
Block 3Previous: 7c1eHash 2b8d

bricks.explanation: Block 3 still stores 7c1e, Block 2's old hash. It no longer matches the new 9f04, so the break shows up right after the edit.

bricks.prompt: Leo edited Block 2 in his copy of a 10-block chain. To make every link in his copy match again, which blocks must he redo?

options.text: Block 2, then every block after it, up to Block 10
Only Block 2
options.feedback: Block 3 still stores Block 2's old hash, so that link stays broken.

options.text: Only Blocks 2 and 3
options.feedback: Updating Block 3's stored link changes Block 3's own hash, which breaks Block 4's link, and so on to the end.

options.text: Blocks 1 and 2
options.feedback: Block 1 comes before the edit and doesn't store Block 2's hash, so it's unaffected.

bricks.hint: When Block 3's stored link changes, what happens to Block 3's own hash?
bricks.explanation:
Each fix changes that block's hash, which breaks the next link.
Block 3 changes, so Block 4 must too, and so on up to Block 10.

bricks.title: Many copies, each checked
bricks.body: Nobody owns a master copy. Many computers, called **nodes** (thousands, for Bitcoin), each keep the whole chain. Every node checks each new block itself: are the records allowed, and does the link match? Blocks that fail are rejected. And a rewritten history on one computer doesn't match the chain everyone else keeps and builds on, so the network ignores it.

term.definition: A computer that keeps its own full copy of the blockchain and checks new blocks.

visual.html:
Node AOriginal chain
Node BOriginal chain
Node COriginal chain
Node DRewritten: ignored
visual.alt: Four nodes. Nodes A, B, and C hold the original chain; Node D holds a rewritten copy, which is marked as ignored.

bricks.prompt: Mia's node receives a version of the chain in which an old payment was changed, and the links no longer match. What does her node do?

options.text: Rejects it and keeps the chain it already has
Accepts it, since it arrived most recently
options.feedback: Newer isn't better. Every node checks what it receives, and broken links fail that check.

options.text: Asks the company that runs the blockchain
options.feedback: There's no company with a master copy. Each node does the checking itself.

bricks.hint: What does every node do with blocks it receives?
bricks.explanation: Mia's node checks the links itself. They don't match, so it rejects that version and keeps its own copy.

bricks.prompt: What makes it so hard to secretly change an old record on a blockchain?

options.text: Each block stores the hash of the block before it
Many nodes each keep and check their own copy
One trusted administrator approves every change
options.feedback: There's no single owner. The protection comes from the links and from the many nodes that check them.

options.text: The records are scrambled so nobody can read them
options.feedback: Hiding records isn't what stops edits. An edit is caught by broken links and by nodes that compare it with their own copy.

bricks.hint: Think about how the blocks connect, and about who keeps them.
bricks.explanation: The links make any edit visible, and the many checking nodes ignore a copy that doesn't match theirs. Together, they keep old records in place.

challenge.prompt: Leo edits an old record to hide that he borrowed the club camera. Then he redoes every later block on his laptop, so all his links match. Does the club's record change?

options.text: No: the other nodes keep the original chain and ignore his copy
Yes: every link in his copy now matches, so it passes
options.feedback: Matching links make his copy consistent, but it still differs from the chain every other node keeps and builds on, so it's ignored.

options.text: Yes: his edit spreads to the other copies automatically
options.feedback: Nodes don't take edits from one computer. Each one keeps its own copy and checks anything new against it.

options.text: Only if he also redoes the newest block
options.feedback: He already redid every later block, the newest included. His copy still doesn't match everyone else's chain.

challenge.hint: Fixing his links solves one problem. What about everyone else's copies?
challenge.explanation: His links match, but his history differs from the chain every other node keeps and builds on. The network ignores it, so the camera record stays.

takeaways: A hash is a block's fingerprint: change anything inside and it comes out completely different.
Each block stores the previous block's hash, so editing one block breaks every link after it.
Many nodes keep and check their own copy, so one computer's rewritten history gets ignored.
